questions.prompt: How many molecules are in \(0.400\,\mathrm{mol}\) of a substance? Use \(N_A=6.02\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).
A substance has molar mass \(5.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\). Find the mass of one molecule.
A sample contains \(3.01\times10^{23}\) molecules. Find the amount in moles.
Find the mass of \(2.5\,\mathrm{mol}\) of a substance with molar mass \(1.8\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\).
A gas sample has \(n=0.80\,\mathrm{mol}\), molar mass \(2.8\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\), and volume \(0.020\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Find its density.
A container of volume \(1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}\) contains \(2.0\times10^{22}\) molecules. Estimate the average molecular spacing using \(r\sim(V/N)^{1/3}\).
A material has density \(900\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) and molar mass \(0.060\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\). Estimate its molecular number density \(N/V\).
questions.answer:
The amount per volume is
\[
\frac{n}{V}=\frac{\rho}{M}
=\frac{900}{0.060}=1.5\times10^4\,\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{N}{V}=\frac{n}{V}N_A
=(1.5\times10^4)(6.02\times10^{23})
=9.0\times10^{27}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}
\]

questions.prompt: Explain, in molecular terms, why a gas is much more compressible than a liquid.
questions.answer: In a gas, molecules are separated by distances much larger than their molecular size, so reducing the volume mostly reduces empty space between molecules. In a liquid, molecules are already close together with little empty space, and intermolecular repulsion rises strongly if they are pushed much closer. That makes liquids far less compressible.

questions.prompt: A substance has molecular mass \(m_0\) and number density \(N/V\). Derive its mass density \(\rho\) in terms of these microscopic quantities, then rewrite it using molar mass \(M\) and moles per volume \(n/V\).
questions.answer:
The total mass is the number of molecules times the mass per molecule:
\[
m=Nm_0
\]
Divide by volume:
\[
\rho=\frac{m}{V}=m_0\frac{N}{V}
\]
Using \(m=nM\),
\[
\rho=\frac{nM}{V}=M\frac{n}{V}
\]

questions.prompt: Two samples have the same mass density but molar masses \(M_A\) and \(M_B=4M_A\). Derive the ratio of their number densities and interpret what it implies about average molecular spacing.
questions.answer:
For the same mass density,
\[
\rho=m_0\frac{N}{V}
\]
and \(m_0=M/N_A\), so number density is proportional to \(1/M\):
\[
\frac{(N/V)_B}{(N/V)_A}=\frac{M_A}{M_B}=\frac{1}{4}
\]
Sample B has one quarter the number density. Since spacing scales roughly as \((V/N)^{1/3}\), its average molecular spacing is larger by
\[
4^{1/3}\approx1.6
\]

questions.prompt: Estimate the average molecular spacing in liquid water using \(\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), \(M=1.8\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\), and \(N_A=6.02\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).

A liquid and its vapor have the same molecular mass. If \(\rho_{\mathrm{liquid}}=800\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) and \(\rho_{\mathrm{vapor}}=1.25\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), estimate the ratio of average molecular spacing in the vapor to that in the liquid.
questions.answer:
For the same molecular mass, number density is proportional to mass density:
\[
\frac{(N/V)_{\mathrm{liquid}}}{(N/V)_{\mathrm{vapor}}}
=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{liquid}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{vapor}}}
=\frac{800}{1.25}=640
\]
Average spacing scales as
\[
r\sim (V/N)^{1/3}
\]
so
\[
\frac{r_{\mathrm{vapor}}}{r_{\mathrm{liquid}}}
=640^{1/3}
=8.6
\]
The vapor molecules are roughly \(9\) times farther apart on average.

questions.prompt: A material has density \(1200\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) and molar mass \(0.030\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\). Estimate the number of molecules in \(2.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^3}\).
A gas has number density \(2.5\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). Estimate the average molecular spacing.
questions.answer:
Use
\[
r\sim\left(\frac{V}{N}\right)^{1/3}=\left(\frac{1}{N/V}\right)^{1/3}
\]
Thus
\[
r\sim\left(\frac{1}{2.5\times10^{25}}\right)^{1/3}=3.4\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm m
\]

questions.prompt: A liquid has molecular spacing about \(3.0\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m\). Estimate its molecular number density.
questions.answer:
The spacing estimate is
\[
r\sim\left(\frac{V}{N}\right)^{1/3}
\]
so
\[
\frac{N}{V}\sim\frac{1}{r^3}
\]
With \(r=3.0\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m\),
\[
\frac{N}{V}\sim\frac{1}{(3.0\times10^{-10})^3}=3.7\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}
\]

questions.prompt: Derive \(m_0=M/N_A\) and explain why molar mass must be in \(\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\) for SI calculations.
questions.answer:
One mole contains \(N_A\) molecules and has mass \(M\). Therefore the mass per molecule is
\[
m_0=\frac{M}{N_A}
\]
If mass is needed in SI equations, \(M\) must be in \(\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\), because the result then has units of kilograms per molecule.

questions.prompt: Use number density to explain why gases have low density compared with liquids made of similar molecules.
questions.answer:
For similar molecules, mass density is
\[
\rho=m_0\frac{N}{V}
\]
The molecular mass \(m_0\) is similar, so density mainly follows number density. Gas molecules are much farther apart, so \(N/V\) is far smaller than in a liquid, giving much lower mass density.

questions.prompt: Two materials have the same number density, but molecule B has twice the molecular mass of molecule A. Compare their mass densities.
questions.answer:
Mass density is
\[
\rho=m_0\frac{N}{V}
\]
If \(N/V\) is the same and \(m_{0,B}=2m_{0,A}\), then
\[
\rho_B=2\rho_A
\]
The denser material has the heavier molecules.

questions.prompt: Explain why molecular spacing estimates are order-of-magnitude models, not exact nearest-neighbor distances.
questions.answer: The estimate assigns each molecule an average volume \(V/N\) and turns that volume into a length scale. Real materials have molecular shapes, correlations, empty spaces, and fluctuating positions, so the estimate gives a useful scale rather than a precise geometric distance.

questions.prompt: Connect molecular kinetic energy and intermolecular forces to the qualitative difference between solid, liquid, and gas.
questions.answer: In solids, intermolecular forces keep molecules near fixed equilibrium positions. In liquids, forces keep short-range spacing but allow rearrangement. In gases, kinetic energy dominates over long-range binding except during collisions, so molecules move freely through much of the container.
